Learning Objectives
Identify commonly encountered bone and soft-tissue tumors of uncertain origin and
pathogenesis.
Describe the clinical presentation of patients with tumors of uncertain origin.
Explain the epidemiology, etiology, and natural history of tumors of uncertain origin.
Describe the radiographic and histologic characteristics that define tumors of unknown origin.
Recognize differences in the diagnosis, surgical management, adjuvant treatment, and
outcomes of different tumors of unknown origin.
Simple Bone Cyst
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy

Overview
Simple bone cysts are benign lesions of early life that may be found incidentally or after
fracture.1
Although clinical presentation may appear similar to that of malignancy, management differs
substantially.1 Rates of local recurrence are high2 (Resource 1).

Overview
A simple bone cyst, also known as a unicameral or essential bone cyst, is a benign fluid-
filled intramedullary cavitary lesion.1,2 Patients may present with pain, swelling, or
pathologic fracture; imaging studies reveal a typically solitary metaphyseal-diaphyseal
lucency without bone expansion or marginal sclerosis.1,2 Recurrence is reported as 10%
to 20%. Outcomes may include growth arrest, osteonecrosis, and spontaneous
resolution.2
Epidemiology
Simple bone cysts favor patients aged 0 to 20 years and are more common in males.2

Epidemiology
A male predominance (3:1 ratio) of simple bone cysts is noted, with approximately 85%
of patients being younger than 20 years; lesions typically are solitary.1,2 Simple bone
cysts account for approximately 3% of all biopsied bone tumors, with common locations
including the femur and proximal humerus.3 (Resource 2)
Anatomy and Biomechanics
Simple bone cysts are benign, hollow lesions that often are filled with serous or
serosanguineous fluid and typically are found in the metaphyseal regions of skeletally

9/4/26, 9:58 AM
AAOS | Tumors of Unknown Origin
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004047
2/22

immature long bones.2,3 .
Etiology
Etiology remains controversial.
Proposed etiologies include intraosseous synovial cysts, traumatic response, and disordered
venous circulation in cancellous bone.3-6
Natural History
Natural history varies by cyst activity; however, prognosis is difficult to determine.

Natural History
Cyst activity may decrease to quiescence and eventually involution.3 If cysts are
asymptomatic or management is not pursued, they may shrink with increasing skeletal
maturity and eventually spontaneously heal.2,3 This course is supported by the rarity of
simple bone cysts in adulthood; however, high cyst activity may lead to recurrence and
possible fracture.2,3 Factors such as age, previous fracture, or cyst site or size have not
been proven to be prognostic.3 Similarly, no evidence shows risk of progression to
malignancy or other bony lesion.3
Classification
Simple bone cysts may be classified as active or latent.
Cysts are considered active if their location is within 1 cm of the physis. They migrate to a
diaphyseal location over time and then are considered latent lesions.7
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History
Often present in children after low-energy trauma resulting in pathologic fracture.

9/4/26, 9:58 AM

Physical Examination
Simple bone cysts often are found incidentally on imaging studies.
Symptoms usually are the result of an associated fracture.
Patients may present with pain accompanied by localized tenderness and swelling or
nondisplaced pathologic fracture.2,3,7
Fractures rarely involve the growth plate.3
Imaging Studies
Radiographs are the mainstay of imaging for simple bone cysts.
CT and MRI usually are unnecessary but may provide additional diagnostic value.
Little, if any, role exists for bone scintigraphy or positron emission tomography/CT in patients
with a simple bone cyst.1
Radiography
Plain radiography is first-line imaging modality for symptomatic patients and is associated with
excellent diagnostic accuracy.7

Radiography
Radiographs typically reveal a juxtaphyseal lucency on the metaphysis of a long bone
without bony expansion or marginal sclerosis.1,2 Cortical thinning is common; however,
the cortex is intact, except in patients with a pathologic fracture.2 Dependent settling of
a small bony fragment within the lesion (fallen leaf sign) is considered pathognomonic
for a simple bone cyst.1,8 A gas bubble in the nondependent margin of a fractured lesion
(rising bubble sign) also may been observed; both denote the presence of a hollow
lesion.9
Computed Tomography
CT may be used to assess the spine and pelvis, to evaluate cyst wall thickness, and to rule out
pathologic fracture.1
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:58 AM
AAOS | Tumors of Unknown Origin
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004047
4/22

Magnetic Resonance Imaging
MRI may confirm the presence of intralesional fluid and reveal more aggressive features, such
as cortical thinning and erosion.1,2,7
Diagnosis
Diagnosis may be made based on radiographic features.7,10
Plain radiography traditionally has been used; however, MRI improves fluid visualization and
evaluation of fracture risk.3,10,11
Differential Diagnosis
Differential diagnosis is highly important because management varies with diagnosis.
Differential diagnoses include aneurysmal bone cyst (ABC), fibrous dysplasia, and
enchondroma.3,10 Distinct radiographic characteristics of each condition help differentiate
respective lesions.10
Management
The management of a simple bone cyst is controversial but only indicated in a narrowly
defined context.
If management is deemed necessary, surgical management is more widely accepted than
injection therapy.
Nonsurgical Management
Observation is appropriate for cysts without concerning features.3
Injection therapy is a controversial and inconsistent treatment option.
Close observation may be used for asymptomatic patients and those able to function
normally in whom bone strength is predominantly preserved;3,10 however, asymptomatic
patients at high risk for progression to fracture, such as those with cysts in the
subtrochanteric femur, may be advised to undergo treatment.3
Methylprednisolone injections have not been reliably shown to be helpful and are associated
with high recurrence rates.10,12,13 Autologous bone marrow injection has inconsistently
resulted in improved cyst resolution. Local recurrence rates are reportedly lower compared
SEND FEEDBACK

5/22

with that after steroid injection; however, poor standardization of outcome definitions make
studies difficult to interpret.10,14,15
Surgical Management
Symptomatic patients or those with an actively enlarging cyst are surgical candidates.
Resection or curettage accompanied by bone grafting typically is the preferred treatment
option.3

Surgical Management
Patients with pathologic fracture, an actively enlarging cyst, or substantial bone fragility
secondary to the cyst are candidates for surgical treatment. Traditional surgical
management involves cyst resection or intralesional curettage followed by bone
grafting.3,10 More recently, methods involving decompression and instrumentation have
been reported.10 Reports of high recurrence rates after surgical management have been
attributed to the selection bias of aggressive, active cysts.3 If a pathologic fracture has
already occurred, the fracture should be allowed to heal before attempting surgical
management.
Complications
Predominant complication of simple bone cyst is recurrence and associated pathologic
fracture.3
Physeal disruption in skeletally immature individuals is uncommon but has been reported.
Morbidity associated with surgical management or repeated fracture secondary to a
recurrent simple bone cyst may be substantial for young patients and their families.3 Physeal
arrest has been reported but has not led to functional limitations.16
Outcomes
Simple bone cysts typically resolve with skeletal maturation.

Given that simple bone cyst prognosis may be difficult to determine, except in patients with
an obvious fracture or bone fragility, and because incidence in adulthood is low, medical or
surgical management should be weighed against the likelihood of eventual cyst
resolution.3,10
Aneurysmal Bone Cyst
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Overview
An ABC is a benign hemorrhagic osteolytic lesion that affects patients aged 0 to 20 years.1,2
An ABC is a benign, cystic lesion with blood interspersed between connective tissue septa.2 It
may be a primary lesion or secondary to a hemorrhagic transformation of a benign or
malignant bony tumor.2
Epidemiology
An ABC is a rare condition that typically occurs in a young population.
The incidence of ABC is approximately 0.14 per 100,000 individuals annually, without sex
predominance. Most patients are in their teenage years, with 75% to 90% of cases diagnosed
in patients before age 20 years.1
Anatomy
Common locations for ABC include the metaphysis of long bones, skull, and spine.
The long bones, spine, and pelvis are common locations for ABCs, with particular
involvement of the metaphysis.1 ABCs have a predilection for the posterior arch of the
lumbar vertebrae and are one of the most common neoplasms of the posterior spine.1,17
Etiology
The etiology of ABCs is unclear.
ABCs were originally thought to form in response to local hemorrhage or increased
intraosseous pressure caused by vascular disturbances.17

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004047
7/22

Natural History
The natural course of unmanaged ABCs may be highly variable.1
Quiescent, active, and aggressive types of ABC affect natural history; outcomes range from
self-resolution to bony destruction to rare malignant transformation.1,2,18
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History
Patients report a history of pain and swelling of the affected limb. They also may present after
low-energy injury or report dysesthesias or motor weakness with spinal involvement.
Physical Examination
Pain and swelling are common presenting complaints.
Patients commonly present with pain, swelling, palpable mass, and rarely fracture.17,19
Neurologic deficits may be present if spinal cord or nerve compression is present.2
Imaging Studies
Plain radiographs and MRI are of the most useful in evaluating ABCs.
Radiography
Plain radiographs are first-line imaging study for ABCs.
Radiography reveals radiolucent, expansile metaphyseal lesions with well-defined margins, a
neocortex, cystic cavities, and subperiosteal reaction.1,2 The lesion may often be eccentric.1
Plain radiographs are less helpful for evaluation of the vertebrae.
Magnetic Resonance Imaging
MRI is a helpful adjunct to plain radiography.
Gadolinium-enhancing internal septa and multiple fluid levels are suggestive of ABC.1,2,17
Fluid-fluid levels also may be observed in telangiectatic osteosarcoma, giant cell tumor, and
secondary ABC and, therefore, are not pathognomonic.17

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004047
8/22

Diagnosis
Biopsy with histologic confirmation is required to diagnose ABC.17
Histologic examination reveals hemorrhagic cavities separated by connective tissue septa
and osteoid formation and differentiates ABC from telangiectatic osteosarcoma.17
Differential Diagnosis
Differential diagnosis of ABCs is broad and includes benign lesions, such as chondromyxoid
fibroma, chondroblastoma, giant cell tumor, and telangiectatic osteosarcoma.17
Clinical and radiographic features may help to narrow the differential diagnosis; however,
tissue biopsy is essential, especially to rule out telangiectatic osteosarcoma given its
radiographic similarities.1,17
Management
Management of ABCs traditionally is surgical; however, nonsurgical treatment options exist.
Curopsy has been described as a percutaneous limited curettage of all quadrants of the cyst
with the use of a small curette at the time of needle biopsy. This technique is associated with
a high rate (>80%) of lesion resolution.20
Other treatment options include curettage with bone grafting, cryotherapy, sclerotherapy,
and en bloc resection.17 Although radiation therapy also is effective, the risk of malignant
transformation prevents its common use.1
Nonsurgical Management
Nonsurgical treatment options include sclerotherapy, radionuclide ablation, and arterial
embolization.17
Nonsurgical treatment options avoid the morbidity associated with wide resection but are
associated with risks, such as accidental ischemia.1 Absolute alcohol sclerotherapy has
shown good efficacy without a high complication rate.1
Surgical Management
Surgical treatment options improve the likelihood of a cure but also increase morbidity.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:58 AM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004047
9/22

Curettage with bone grafting is a popular treatment option; however, incomplete resection
may lead to cyst recurrence and necessitate additional management.17 Extended
intralesional curettage and en bloc resection are associated with lower recurrence
rates;17however, recurrence rates as high as 50% have been reported in the in the
literature.21 Therefore, adjuvants, including hydrogen peroxide, phenol, polymethyl
methacrylate, a high-speed burr, or electrocautery, frequently are used.22 Care must be
taken to select patients carefully, especially if performing en bloc resection, to avoid
unnecessary morbidity for a benign condition.1,17
Giant Cell Tumor of Bone
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Overview
A giant cell tumor is a benign, locally aggressive lesion with metastatic potential that usually
involves the epiphyses of long bones. The histogenesis is considered unknown.23
Surgical management is first-line treatment; however, medical therapies also are available.24

Overview
Giant cell tumor is a benign tumor with a propensity for locally aggressive behavior and
metastatic potential that typically is found in the epiphyseal-metaphyseal regions of long
bones, including the distal femur, radius, proximal tibia, humerus and sacrum.2,25
Symptomatic patients typically present in their twenties and thirties.24 Surgical
management via extended intralesional curettage is the mainstay of management.25 The
use of diphosphonates or denosumab is an adjuvant treatment option.24 Local
recurrence is common; pulmonary metastases occur in a small number of patients and
typically are benign in nature.2 The risk of malignant transformation of giant cell tumor is
associated with late local recurrence and radiation therapy.
Epidemiology
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:58 AM
AAOS | Tumors of Unknown Origin
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004047
10/22

Giant cell tumor accounts for 20% of benign bone tumors.2
Giant cell tumor of bone accounts for 4% to 5% of all primary bone tumors and typically is
observed in young adults aged 20 to 40 years.2,25It rarely is observed in skeletally immature
patients; in these rare instances, it tends to be metaphyseal.2 A slight female predominance
has been reported.2,25
Anatomy and Biomechanics
Giant cell tumor typically is found in the epiphysis or epiphyseal-metaphyseal region of long
bones and also may be observed in the sacrum.
Common locations of giant cell tumor include the distal femur, distal radius, proximal tibia,
and proximal humerus.2,24 The most common axial skeleton location is the sacrum, and it
rarely is found in the hands and feet.2,24 Multicentric giant cell tumor is very rare.2,25
Etiology
Giant cell tumor originates from mononuclear cells and exhibits oncogene alterations.24
Giant cell tumor originates from the mononuclear cells responsible for production of type I
and type II collagen rather than its namesake cell.24 Telomeric association and oncogene
alterations also have been noted.2,24
Classification
Giant cell tumors are grouped by stage and classified according to the Campanacci
classification system.26 Rates of local recurrence increase in higher grade lesions.
The Campanacci classification system is based on radiographic appearance of giant cell
tumors of bone. Grade 1 lesions demonstrate no cortical disruption and have well-defined
sclerotic margins, whereas grade 2 lesions are defined by cortical expansion and thinning
and a well-defined non-sclerotic medullary margin. Grade 3 lesions demonstrate unclear
margins, cortical disruption, and soft-tissue extension.26
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Physical Examination

11/22

Patients typically present in their twenties to thirties with activity-related pain and nocturnal
discomfort, soft-tissue swelling, and limitations in range of motion.2,24

Physical Examination
Patients may exhibit tenderness, swelling, range of motion limitations, effusion, or
synovitis.2,24,25 Approximately 5% to 10% of patients present with pathologic fracture,
and fracture lines may reach the articular surface.2,24.
Imaging Studies
Plain radiographs are the first-line imaging study for giant cell tumor. CT and MRI may provide
additional information.

Imaging Studies
 Radiographs typically reveal an expansive radiolucent lesion involving the epiphysis and
metaphysis.2,24 Extension to the subchondral plate and the presence of a periosteal
shell without considerable reactive bone formation may be observed.2,24 CT may
provide additional evidence of cortical thinning and cystic degeneration.2,24 On MRI,
giant cell tumor appears bright on T2-weighted images and may reveal multiple fluid
levels.2,24.
Diagnosis
Radiographs typically demonstrate a very characteristic lesion, and MRI is helpful in
determining biopsy approach and the extent of soft-tissue involvement and in planning for
surgical management.24 Biopsy is required for definitive diagnosis.
Differential Diagnosis
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:58 AM
AAOS | Tumors of Unknown Origin
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004047
12/22

The differential diagnosis includes benign and malignant entities.
ABC, chondroblastoma, osteoblastoma, and chondromyxoid fibroma may have a similar
appearance and are high on the differential diagnosis.
Telangiectatic osteosarcoma always should be considered in the differential diagnosis.
Overlapping radiographic characteristics also are observed in multiple myeloma,
plasmacytoma, giant cell osteosarcoma, clear cell chondrosarcoma, and lytic metastases and
should be considered in the differential diagnosis.24,27
Management
Surgical management is the mainstay of treatment for giant cell tumor; however, medical
adjuncts may be useful in patients with local recurrence and for tumors not amenable to
surgical management.
Nonsurgical Management
Nonsurgical treatment options, such as denosumab, diphosphonates, and radiation therapy,
typically are reserved for tumors considered to be unresectable or in which resection would
result in unacceptable morbidity and for patients who have experienced multiple local
recurrences.
Denosumab, a monoclonal antibody that targets receptor-activated nuclear factor-kappa B
ligand, is effective at reducing the formation and activation of osteoclasts, which decreases
bone loss, prevents tumor regrowth, and decreases the risk of fracture.24,28
Denosumab is indicated if tumors cannot be resected or in patients with severe morbidity
associated with surgical treatment; however, it also has been used in the neoadjuvant and
adjuvant setting.23,29,30
Radiation therapy may be used in challenging areas, such as the sacrum or spine; however,
an associated risk of malignant transformation exists.24
Diphosphonates have been used to help hinder osteoclastic activity and have been shown to
lower recurrence rates if combined with surgical management.24,31
Surgical Management
Surgical management continues to be the primary method of treatment of giant cell tumor;
however, recurrence secondary to incomplete resection must be balanced against morbidity.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:58 AM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004047
13/22

Wide resection previously was a popular option; however, associated morbidity led to
increased and primary use of curettage with adjuvant management, such as cryotherapy.24
En bloc resection may be performed for aggressive tumors or those located in nonessential
bone.24
Outcomes
Local recurrence rates are as high as 20% after surgical management; however, recurrence
may be managed via an additional local procedure.24
Local recurrence typically is observed within 2 years of management; rates are lower with en
bloc resection.2 Benign pulmonary metastases may be observed in approximately 2% to 4%
of patients with a giant cell tumor but often may be managed via resection.2,24
Tenosynovial Giant Cell Tumor
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Overview
Tenosynovial giant cell tumor (TGCT) is a benign neoplastic disease affecting the joints that
encompasses a spectrum of disease, including localized and diffuse variants. 32

Overview
TGCT is characterized by painful joint effusions and proliferation of the synovium or
tendon sheath, which may lead to bony erosions. Previous nomenclature included
pigmented villonodular synovitis, which currently is characterized as diffuse-type TGCT,
and giant cell tumor of the tendon sheath, which currently is termed localized-type TGCT
and found most frequently in the hand.32
Epidemiology
TGCT is a rare condition that most commonly occurs in the knees of younger patients.

9/4/26, 9:58 AM
AAOS | Tumors of Unknown Origin
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004047
14/22

It most commonly occurs in adults aged 30 to 40 years, with a slight female predominance;32
however, it can occur at any age.
Anatomy and Biomechanics
Diffuse-type TGCT most frequently occurs in the knee, whereas the localized type is most
common in the hand.
TGCT most commonly affects the anterior knee but also may occur in the hip, ankle,
shoulder, and elbow.33
Etiology
The pathogenesis of TGCT is controversial but has been linked to overexpression of colony-
stimulating factor 1 (CSF1). 

Etiology
A translocation of t(1p13;2q35) has been identified as leading to overexpression of CSF1,
which results in reactive macrophage activation.34 This overexpression of macrophages
is thought to be the cause of the soft-tissue hyperplasia in the synovium and tendon
sheaths.32
Natural History
TGCT typically follows an insidious course, with progressively worsening pain and swelling over
time. Unmanaged TGCT may result in extensive joint erosion or degenerative changes.
Unmanaged TGCT may result in varying levels of joint destruction and ultimately may lead to
the need for arthroplasty, arthrodesis, or amputation (rare).
Classification
TGCT may present as localized or diffuse disease.32 Previous nomenclature for diffuse-type
TGCT was pigmented villonodular synovitis and for localized-type TGCT was giant cell tumor of

the tendon sheath.
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History
Patients typically present with pain, stiffness, and recurrent atraumatic hemarthroses.
Patients most frequently present with monoarticular, progressively worsening joint pain and
swelling.
Physical Examination
On physical examination, patients may present with a joint effusion, erythema, or limited
range of motion.
Depending on the size or joint involvement, nodules or soft-tissue masses may be palpable
in and around the joint.
Imaging Studies
MRI is the preferred diagnostic and most sensitive imaging modality for identifying this
pathology.33

Imaging Studies
Radiographs may demonstrate nonspecific soft-tissue swelling or a joint effusion but
typically are normal. Late-stage disease may show cystic erosion or joint destruction. MRI
will reveal not only joint effusion but also help visualize the villous or nodular synovial
proliferations. Classically, TGCT is associated with a low signal intensity on all pulse
sequences. A blooming artifact—signal loss of gradient-echo sequences—is the result of
the iron in the extensive hemosiderin depositions present.33
Pathology
Synovial tissue biopsy can definitively confirm diagnosis in cases of uncertainty.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:58 AM
AAOS | Tumors of Unknown Origin
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004047
16/22

Gross appearance typically is villous proliferation of the synovium with a brownish hue from
hemosiderin deposition.35
Low-power magnification will reveal highly vascularized villous synovium with visible
hemosiderin deposits.35
High-power magnification demonstrates many multinucleated giant cells and pigment-laden
macrophages.33
Diagnosis
TGCT diagnosis can be made via MRI, visually during arthroscopy, and ultimately via
histological analysis.
Differential Diagnosis
The radiographic differential diagnosis includes hemophilic arthropathy, hemorrhagic
synovitis, and inflammatory arthropathy.
Other diagnoses to consider are synovial chondromatosis, septic arthritis, or soft-tissue
sarcoma.
Management
Nonsurgical Management
Nonsurgical treatment options include observation and/or pexidartinib (CSF1 receptor
antagonist).
Observation typically is reserved for asymptomatic patients or those who are poor surgical
candidates.
Pexidartinib was approved by the FDA in 2019 for the management of TGCT not likely to
improve with surgical management. It can reduce the length and volume of the tumor;
however, patients’ liver function must be monitored.36
Surgical Management
Surgical treatment options include partial synovectomy, total synovectomy, total synovectomy
and total joint arthroplasty, and total synovectomy and arthrodesis.
Partial arthroscopic synovectomy is indicated for the localized form of TGCT.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:58 AM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004047
17/22

Open, complete synovectomy is indicated in patients who are symptomatic with diffuse
disease.
In patients with advanced bony destruction and joint disease, total synovectomy and total
joint arthroplasty may be offered. In some patients, such as those with severe disease in the
ankle, complete synovectomy and arthrodesis may result in the best outcomes.
Because of the high recurrence rate, adjuvant treatments include the use of intra-articular
radioisotopes and external beam radiation therapy. These have been reported to result in
lower recurrence rates than surgical management alone.37,38
Complications
The most common complication is local recurrence, which has been reported to be as high as
50% for diffuse disease and 15% for localized disease.34,39
Rates of recurrence can be reduced with the addition of external beam radiation therapy or
with the use of pexidartinib.
Joint destruction also may occur because of uncontrolled primary disease or recurrence.
Mark as Complete
